title: 道德經 第六十二章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 62, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 83. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 62 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 為道 (Practising the Way). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: as for — marks off the topic; no verb 'to be' follows
the ten thousand things — everything there is
the sheltered south-west corner of a hall, where the household spirits are honoured; hence a place of shelter and of honour. Wang Bi glosses it 曖 'shade' — what one takes cover under.

sentences.l: The Way — the sheltering recess of the ten-thousand things.
sentences.i: The Way is the inner corner where the ten thousand things are sheltered.
sentences.n:
奧 is a room word before it is a philosophical one: the dark corner of the hall, out of the draught, where the ancestors' seat was set. It is at once the safest place and the place of honour, and both senses are wanted here.

The Mawangdui silk manuscripts read something else entirely — 注, 'that into which all things pour', which is usually taken as standing for 主, 'master'. That gives a Way things flow into or are ruled by, rather than one they shelter in. Our text is Wang Bi's, and his gloss is shelter.

morph.gloss: a treasure, a thing kept and guarded — the graph is jade and cowrie shells under a roof
that which — makes a noun of the verb after it: 'what he ——s'
to keep safe, to hold on to — what preserves him

sentences.l: and what the not-good man keeps hold of.
sentences.n:
善人 and 不善人 are not bound words; they are just 'good man' and 'not-good man', and the reader can see the parts. The pair came up in chapter 27, where the good man is the not-good man's teacher and the not-good man is the good man's stock-in-trade.

The point of the couplet is the second half. The Way is not a reward for the good; the man who is not good has it too, and holds on to it.

所 makes a noun of the object of 保, so what the line says is that the Way is what the not-good man keeps hold of. Wang Bi's gloss on 保 is 全, 'to keep whole', which lets the sentence be turned round in English — the Way as what keeps him whole — but the 所 is the grammar, and we follow it.

sentences.t:
美言可以市，
尊行可以加人。

morph.gloss: can, is able to — with 以 following it, 'can, by this means'
by it, by this — 以 takes the topic as its object: 'by fine words, one can ——'
a market; here the noun used as a verb — to trade, to fetch a price
conduct, the way a man carries himself — the verb 'to walk' as a noun (xíng, not háng 'a row')
can, is able to — with 以 following it, 'can, by this means'
by it, by this — 以 takes the topic as its object: 'by honoured conduct, one can ——'
to add, to lay on top of — to set a man above others

sentences.l:
Fine words can buy in the market;
honoured conduct can be laid on top of a man.
sentences.i: Fine words will buy anything in the market; honoured conduct sets a man above the rest.
sentences.n:
可以 is two words here, not the single modern Mandarin verb: 可 'can' plus 以 'by this'. The subject is the means, not the thing acted on — 'by fine words one can buy', not 'fine words can be sold'. The second line settles it for both: 加人 already has its own object, 人, so 尊行 cannot itself be the thing laid on.

Wang Bi glosses the first line 美言可以奪眾貨之賈 — fine words can outbid the price of every commodity on sale — and takes the second the same way, of conduct reaching other men. The lines sit oddly in a book that distrusts fine words, and the argument depends on that oddity: if even the cheap goods of speech and reputation buy that much, the Way is beyond pricing.

sentences.t:
人之不善，
何棄之有？

morph.gloss: of — the genitive turning the clause into a noun, 'a man's not-being-good'
casting off, throwing away (the verb standing as the fronted object of 有)
— here 之 is neither 'of' nor 'him': it props the fronted object in place before the verb

sentences.l:
A man's not-being-good —
what casting-off is there?
sentences.i: And if a man is not good — why should he be thrown away?
sentences.n:
何棄之有 is a set construction and worth learning whole. Plain order would be 有何棄, 'there is what casting-off?'. Classical Chinese pulls an interrogative object in front of its verb and pins it there with 之, which here is doing a third job — not the genitive 'of', not the pronoun 'him', but a hinge. Whenever you see 何 … 之 有, unwind it that way.

Some read 之 as the plain object pronoun instead ('what throwing-away of him is there'), which comes to nearly the same English by a different route.

The question is rhetorical and answers chapter 27's 無棄人, 'no one is thrown away'.

morph.gloss: to set up, to install — of a ruler, to enthrone
the Son of Heaven — the king, who holds his mandate from heaven
to set in place, to appoint to office
the Three Dukes — the three highest offices of state, the ministers standing next to the king
a duke; impartial, belonging to all alike

sentences.l:
Therefore at the setting up of the Son of Heaven,
at the installing of the Three Dukes,
sentences.i: So when the Son of Heaven is enthroned and the Three Dukes installed,
sentences.n:
Two clauses that are not yet the main clause. 立 and 置 are verbs, but nothing is asserted of them: they set the scene for what comes next, and Chinese leaves the hinge unmarked where English needs 'when'. The sentence does not close until the following unit.

天子 and 三公 are both fixed terms of state, so each is one tap-unit here even though the parts are ordinary words.

sentences.t:
雖有拱璧以先駟馬，
不如坐進此道。

morph.gloss: a jade disc so large it takes both arms to hold — the most precious of formal presents
to fold both arms round; the span of two arms
a flat ring of jade, the ceremonial gift of the highest rank
to go before, to be sent ahead of — the adverb 'first' used as a verb
a team of four horses drawing one chariot — the grandest of gifts
a team of four horses yoked to one chariot
to come up to, to be the equal of — 不如 X, 'is not as good as X'
to sit — here 'while merely sitting', without stirring
to offer forward, to present — the verb 'to advance' used transitively

sentences.l:
though there be the arms-full jade sent ahead of a team of four horses,
it is not the equal of sitting still and offering forward this Way.
sentences.i: though a great jade be presented before a team of four horses, that is nothing beside sitting still and offering this Way.
sentences.n:
以先駟馬 is court protocol, not speed: at a state presentation the jade goes in first and the horses follow behind it. The two together were about the most expensive thing one ruler could hand another, and the whole point of naming them is that they are named at the enthronement.

坐 is doing adverbial work — 'seated', that is, without getting up, without effort, without a procession. The contrast is between an occasion and a man who does not stir.

sentences.t:
古之所以貴此道者何？
不曰以求得，
有罪以免邪？
故為天下貴。

morph.gloss: that whereby, the means by which — classically the how of a thing, not the modern Mandarin 'therefore'
that which — makes a noun of the verb after it
to prize, to set a high price on — the adjective 'costly' used as a verb
the one that — it closes the topic and the question hangs on it
what? — the interrogative standing last, as the whole predicate
by it — that is, by the Way
to seek, to go looking for
an offence, guilt — a crime and the punishment owed for it
to be let off, to escape punishment, to be pardoned
— the final particle making the whole a rhetorical question, 'is it not?' (yé; read xié it means 'crooked')
to be, to count as — read wéi, the plain verb, not the benefactive wèi
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it

sentences.l:
That whereby the ancients prized this Way — what was it?
Did they not say: by it one seeks and gets,
having offences, by it one is let off?
Therefore it counts as all under heaven's precious thing.
sentences.i: What was it that made the ancients prize this Way? Did they not say: seek by it and you find; be guilty, and by it you are pardoned? That is why it is what all under heaven holds precious.
sentences.n:
所以 …者何 is the standard classical way of asking why: 'the-means-by-which they prized it — what?' The question word sits at the end because it is the whole answer-slot, and 者 holds everything before it together as one long topic.

Many editions print 求以得 rather than 以求得 in the first of the two quoted clauses, which balances it against 有罪以免 and reads 'seek, and by it get'. The sense is the same either way.

The last five characters repeat the closing line of chapter 56 exactly — the same words, in the same place, ending a chapter. This is one of the book's stitched seams, and there are several.
